lessons.title: Resource accounts for voice apps
lessons.why: The attendant and the queue are not callable until an account represents them.
body: Create the resource account, assign the Teams Phone Resource Account license, and attach it to the attendant or queue. A phone number is optional until the PSTN must reach that app. The account stays disabled for sign-in.

At least one Teams Phone license in the tenant turns on the voice-app services. A tenant with zero phone-system licenses will not grow a working queue out of a resource account alone. Read the prerequisite article for the current wording.

flow.label: Number
flow.detail: Only if PSTN must reach it

lessons.say: The resource account is the voice app’s identity. The number is optional until you publish it.
lessons.fault: The queue exists and has no licensed resource account, so it never answers.
lessons.listen: Every attendant and queue that answers needs a licensed resource account. Add a phone number only if the PSTN must reach it.

lessons.title: Auto attendant design
lessons.why: The published company number is usually this object. A sloppy menu is a public defect.
body: Set business hours, holidays, a greeting you have rights to play, menu keys, directory search scope, and an operator. Directory search will find people you did not mean to publish if you leave it wide open.

Each menu key needs a target: a person, a queue, another attendant, voicemail, or an external number. External targets need funding. A key that points nowhere is a silent failure with your logo on it.
lessons.say: Hours, holidays, greeting, scoped directory, and an operator. Every key has a target.
lessons.fault: The office is closed on a holiday and the attendant still hunts a queue.
lessons.listen: Design the attendant’s hours, holidays, greeting, menu targets, and operator before you publish the number.

lessons.title: Queue routing methods
lessons.why: Attendant, serial, round robin, and longest idle are different promises to the people answering.
body: Attendant routing rings available agents together. Serial walks a list. Round robin remembers the last agent. Longest idle offers the call to the person waiting longest. Presence-based routing can skip someone who is already in a call or a meeting.

Conference mode changes whether the caller sits in a conference while agents are tried. Test it with two agents, one busy, before you argue about delay. An opt-out flag without a workforce plan means the schedule and the queue disagree by lunchtime.

chart.title: Methods
chart.note: Four documented methods. Not a quality score.

lessons.say: I can define the four routing methods and I will test presence with two agents.
lessons.fault: Serial routing pins every call on the first person, who then opts out.
lessons.listen: Pick attendant, serial, round robin, or longest idle on purpose, then test with one agent busy.

lessons.why: A queue without overflow is a waiting room with a locked door.
body: Set a timeout that a human would tolerate, and an overflow target: another queue, a person, voicemail, or an external number. Voicemail overflow needs a mailbox. External overflow, callback, and on-behalf outbound need pay-as-you-go or communications credits on the resource account.
Callback is an outbound call. A greeting that promises a callback you cannot fund is a falsehood with a phone number on it. Test overflow by making every agent busy, not by reading the setting.
lessons.say: Overflow is a target I have tested. External overflow is funded.
lessons.fault: Callback is enabled and every return call fails because nothing was funded.
lessons.listen: Give every queue a timeout and an overflow you have tested. Fund the resource account if it dials out.

lessons.title: Nested voice apps
lessons.why: Real companies are a tree: one attendant, a few queues, an overflow attendant. The tree needs a picture.
body: An attendant can send a key to a queue. A queue can overflow to another queue or back to an attendant. Draw it. If you cannot draw it, callers will find the loop before you do.
Keep one published pilot number. Internal targets do not each need a ported number. A design that ports a number per menu key is paying carrier lead time for a diagram.

flow.label: Overflow
flow.detail: Back to a person or voicemail

lessons.say: One pilot number, a drawn tree, no loops, overflow that ends.
lessons.fault: Menu key 1 points at a queue whose overflow points back at the same menu.
lessons.listen: Draw nested attendants and queues. Publish one pilot number, and make sure overflow ends.

lessons.title: Numbers on voice apps
lessons.why: The number’s owner decides whether the company keeps it when a human leaves.
body: Put service numbers on resource accounts. Do not put the main number on a receptionist’s user object. Caller ID for the queue should be chosen, not inherited from whoever built the queue.

How you get the number depends on the connectivity option: Microsoft inventory, the Operator Connect carrier, or the Direct Routing carrier. Porting is a carrier project with a date, not a PowerShell metaphor.

chart.title: Who should own the main number
chart.note: The resource account, not a person.

lessons.say: Service numbers sit on resource accounts. Caller ID is a choice.
lessons.fault: The receptionist leaves and the main number is released with their user.
lessons.listen: Assign the company number to a resource account, and set caller ID on purpose.
